title: Coalition survives late-night confidence vote after junior partner backs budget
summary: Prime Minister Odalys Kerrow won the vote 164 to 151 after the Progressive Union secured last-minute concessions on rail funding and childcare, ending a week of uncertainty in Halden.
author: Elsabet Varrow
imageCaption: Prime Minister Odalys Kerrow leaves the parliament building in Halden shortly after the vote.
body: Prime Minister Odalys Kerrow’s coalition survived a confidence vote shortly after midnight on Tuesday, after the junior Progressive Union party agreed to back her budget in exchange for an expanded rail investment package and a phased increase in childcare subsidies.

The motion passed 164 to 151, with four members abstaining. It was the closest margin the government has faced since it took office two years ago, and it came after a week in which senior figures on both sides had openly discussed the possibility of an early election.

Under the agreement, the government will bring forward $2.4 billion in spending on regional rail lines, including the long-delayed electrification of the Calloway corridor. Childcare subsidies will rise by 15 per cent from April, with a second increase tied to next year’s growth figures.
In return, the Progressive Union dropped its demand for a windfall levy on energy companies, a measure the finance ministry had warned would deter investment in offshore wind projects.

body.quote: We did not come into government to bring it down. We came in to change what it does, and tonight we changed it.
body.by: Tamsin Rookhaven, leader of the Progressive Union

body: Opposition leader Barnaby Quell called the agreement “a ransom note dressed up as a budget” and said his National Reform party would table amendments when the finance bill reaches committee stage next month.

Bond markets, which had sold off sharply on Friday amid fears of political deadlock, were largely unmoved in early trading. Analysts at Brennick Capital said the result removed “the immediate tail risk” but warned that the coalition’s slim majority would make further fiscal tightening difficult.
The finance bill is expected to return to the chamber in early December. Ms Kerrow is due to address parliament on Wednesday afternoon.

title: Northwind Freight to cut 1,200 jobs as container rates slide to four-year low
summary: The logistics group will close two depots and consolidate its operations at Port Ardley, blaming weak demand and overcapacity across global shipping lanes.
author: Teodor Quillane
imageCaption: Containers stacked at Northwind Freight’s terminal in Port Ardley.
body: Northwind Freight, one of the country’s largest logistics operators, said on Tuesday it would cut about 1,200 jobs over the next nine months as falling container rates and weaker consumer demand squeeze margins across the industry.

The company will close depots in Brennick and Ashford Vale and move most of its warehousing to an expanded site at Port Ardley, where it has invested heavily in automated sorting over the past three years.

Chief executive Sorrel Imbry said the decision was “painful but unavoidable”. Spot rates for a standard 40-foot container on the company’s busiest routes have fallen by roughly 38 per cent since January, according to industry data.

body.quote: We built for a world that was shipping more every year. That world has paused, and we have to be honest about it.
body.by: Sorrel Imbry, chief executive of Northwind Freight

body: The Transport and General Workers’ Union said it would seek urgent talks and accused management of using automation as cover for cost-cutting. About a third of the affected roles are in driving, with the rest in warehousing and administration.
Shares in Northwind fell 4.2 per cent in afternoon trading. The company also cut its full-year profit guidance for the second time since the summer.

title: Lumen Systems pauses rollout of workplace assistant after data-retention complaints
summary: The software company said it would review how long its Atlas AI tool keeps employee conversations, after three large customers raised concerns with regulators.
author: Ilsa Marrowby
imageCaption: Lumen Systems’ headquarters in Westmere.
body: Lumen Systems has paused the wider rollout of Atlas, its AI workplace assistant, after several corporate customers complained that the tool was storing employee conversations for longer than their contracts allowed.

The company said in a statement on Tuesday that a configuration error had caused some chat logs to be retained for up to 18 months instead of the 30 days customers had selected. It said there was no evidence the data had been accessed by unauthorised parties.
At least three customers, including a regional bank and a hospital group, have referred the matter to the Data Protection Office, according to two people familiar with the complaints.

body.h: A setback at a sensitive moment

body: The pause comes weeks after Lumen told investors that Atlas would be its main source of revenue growth next year. The company had signed up more than 900 business customers since the product launched in March.
“Trust is the entire product here,” said Ines Vossberg, an analyst at Westmere Research. “If customers can’t be sure where their staff’s conversations end up, the features don’t matter.”
Lumen said the rollout would resume once an external audit had been completed, which it expects to take about six weeks.

title: Bond yields climb as traders bet on one more rate rise before spring
summary: The ten-year yield touched 4.38 per cent, its highest since July, after stronger-than-expected wage data and hawkish comments from the central bank’s deputy governor.
author: Corwin Ashgrove
imageCaption: Traders on the floor of the Halden exchange on Tuesday morning.
body: Government borrowing costs rose for a third consecutive session on Tuesday as investors increased bets that the central bank will raise interest rates once more before the end of the first quarter.

The yield on the ten-year bond climbed eight basis points to 4.38 per cent, the highest level since July. Two-year yields, which are more sensitive to expectations for monetary policy, rose 11 basis points to 4.71 per cent.
The moves followed data showing average weekly earnings grew 5.6 per cent in the three months to September, well above the 4.9 per cent forecast by economists.

Speaking at a conference in Halden, deputy governor Wilma Tessaly said the bank “cannot yet be confident” that inflation would return to target without further action. Money markets now price a roughly 70 per cent chance of a quarter-point rise in February.
Equities were mixed. The MLX 100 index ended the day 0.6 per cent higher, lifted by banks, while housebuilders fell on concerns that higher mortgage rates would weigh on demand.

title: Fishing nations agree to cut North Atlantic mackerel quota after three-week standoff
summary: Negotiators settled on a 12 per cent reduction for next year, ending a dispute that had threatened to close ports to rival fleets.
author: Maren Oakhollow
imageCaption: Fishing boats moored in harbour ahead of the new season.
body: Five coastal states agreed early on Tuesday to cut the total catch of North Atlantic mackerel by 12 per cent next year, ending a three-week standoff that had threatened to spill into a wider trade dispute.

The deal, reached after a final 19-hour session of talks in Bergen, sets the combined quota at roughly 690,000 tonnes and introduces, for the first time, a shared system for reporting catches in near real time.
Scientists had recommended a deeper cut of nearly 20 per cent, warning that stocks had declined for five consecutive years as warmer waters pushed the fish further north.

body.quote: Nobody leaves this room happy, which is usually the sign of a fair agreement.
body.by: Halvar Senne, chair of the negotiations

body: Environmental groups welcomed the reporting rules but said the reduction did not go far enough. Fishing industry associations, meanwhile, warned that smaller boats would struggle to stay viable.
The agreement still needs to be ratified by each government, a process officials expect to complete before the new fishing season opens in January.

title: Deep-sea survey finds cold-water coral reef twice the size previously thought
summary: Researchers mapping the Calder Shelf say the reef stretches for almost 90 kilometres, making it one of the largest of its kind ever recorded.
author: Saffi Underly
imageCaption: An autonomous survey vehicle is lowered from the research ship Halcyon.
body: A cold-water coral reef off the Calder Shelf is roughly twice as large as previously estimated, according to a new survey that used autonomous underwater vehicles to map the seabed in unprecedented detail.

The reef, which lies between 400 and 700 metres below the surface, stretches for almost 90 kilometres. Earlier surveys, conducted with ship-based sonar in the 2010s, had put its length at around 40 kilometres.

The team from the National Oceanographic Institute spent 31 days at sea, deploying two vehicles that each operated for up to 20 hours at a time. They captured more than 600,000 images, which are now being analysed with the help of volunteer citizen scientists.

Cold-water corals grow extremely slowly, often less than a centimetre a year, and parts of the reef are thought to be several thousand years old. They provide habitat for hundreds of species, including commercially important fish.
“We are still discovering basic facts about places like this,” said Dr Imogen Pellow, who led the expedition. “You cannot protect what you haven’t mapped.”
The institute has recommended that the newly mapped sections be added to an existing marine protected area, a proposal the environment ministry said it would consider.

title: Westmere Rovers stun league leaders with stoppage-time winner
summary: Teenage substitute Kip Wendlow scored his first senior goal in the 94th minute to end Calloway City’s 14-match unbeaten run.
author: Bram Kettleby
imageCaption: Rovers players celebrate at the final whistle at Riverside Park.
body: Kip Wendlow, an 18-year-old who had been on the pitch for less than ten minutes, scored in the fourth minute of stoppage time as Westmere Rovers beat league leaders Calloway City 2-1 at Riverside Park on Monday night.

It was Wendlow’s first goal in senior football, and it ended City’s unbeaten run of 14 matches in all competitions. The defeat leaves City two points clear at the top, with Brennick United now level on games played.
City had led through Rufus Gallard’s header shortly before half-time, but Rovers equalised in the 71st minute when captain Owen Marrick converted a penalty after a handball in the area.
The winner came from a corner that City failed to clear. Wendlow’s first shot was blocked, but he reacted quickest to the rebound and drove the ball in off the underside of the bar.

body.quote: I don’t really remember it. I just remember everyone landing on top of me.

body: Rovers manager Elise Vantorre said the result showed her side “can compete with anyone on a good night”. Rovers move up to sixth, three points outside the qualifying places.

title: Hospitals in three regions report early start to winter flu season
summary: Admissions for influenza have doubled in a fortnight, prompting health officials to urge eligible groups to get vaccinated before December.
author: Oriel Thistlecombe
imageCaption: A pharmacist prepares vaccines at a walk-in clinic in Halden.
body: Hospitals in the northern, coastal and capital regions are reporting an unusually early rise in flu admissions, with health officials warning that the season could peak several weeks earlier than usual.

According to figures published by the Public Health Agency on Tuesday, 1,184 patients were admitted with confirmed influenza in the week to Sunday, more than double the number two weeks earlier. At the same point last year, weekly admissions were below 400.
The dominant strain this year is H3N2, which tends to cause more severe illness in older people. Officials said the current vaccine appeared to be a good match.
Uptake among people over 65 stands at 58 per cent, compared with 66 per cent at this stage last year. Among eligible children, the figure is lower still.

“The single most useful thing people can do this week is book their jab,” said Dr Desmond Farrowby, the agency’s director of immunisation. “It takes about two weeks to build protection, and we are already seeing the virus spread.”
Several hospital trusts have reopened winter wards early and asked visitors with cold or flu symptoms to stay away.

title: A forgotten modernist finally gets her retrospective, 40 years after her death
summary: The National Gallery’s survey of Vera Asterholm’s paintings, many unseen since the 1960s, makes a persuasive case that she was a generation ahead of her peers.
author: Livia Merrowind
imageCaption: Visitors at a preview of “Vera Asterholm: The Quiet Line” at the National Gallery.
body: For most of the past four decades, the paintings of Vera Asterholm have lived in storerooms, private hallways and, in at least one case, a garden shed in Ashford Vale. The National Gallery’s new retrospective, which opens to the public on Friday, brings 112 of them together for the first time.

Asterholm, who died in 1986, exhibited only twice during her lifetime. Her large, flat fields of colour, often cut through by a single dark line, were dismissed by critics of the day as “decorative”. Seen now, they look startlingly modern.

The exhibition is arranged chronologically, beginning with small, careful still lifes from the late 1940s and building toward the vast canvases she made in a converted boathouse in the 1960s. The final room, which contains just three paintings, is the strongest gallery space I have seen this year.

body.quote: She wasn’t overlooked because the work was difficult. She was overlooked because nobody was looking.

body: There are gaps. Her letters, which are quoted throughout the wall texts, suggest a body of work on paper that is barely represented here. But this is a show that corrects a long injustice, and it does so with care.
Vera Asterholm: The Quiet Line runs at the National Gallery, Halden, until 28 March.

title: The budget fixes the arithmetic. It doesn’t fix the trust problem.
summary: The coalition has bought itself time. Unless it explains what it is for, that time will be spent fighting the next crisis.
author: Fenn Hollowmere
imageCaption: The parliament building in Halden at dusk.
body: Last night’s vote was a relief for the government, and for anyone holding government bonds. It should not be mistaken for a vote of confidence in any meaningful sense of the word.

The numbers in the budget broadly add up. The rail money is overdue, and the childcare increase will help families who have been squeezed for three years. But the way the deal was reached, in a series of late-night calls and leaked ultimatums, tells voters something the spreadsheets don’t.
It tells them that the coalition’s priorities are set by whichever partner is most willing to walk away. That is not a governing philosophy. It is a negotiating posture.

Ms Kerrow has two years left of her term. She could use the next few months to set out, plainly, three or four things her government intends to finish before the next election, and then report on them in public every quarter.
That sounds modest, and it is. But trust in politics is rarely rebuilt by grand gestures. It is rebuilt by people doing what they said they would do, and being seen to do it.
The alternative is another winter of brinkmanship, and another vote that the government might not win.

title: Opposition demands inquiry into Harbour Bridge contract overruns
summary: Documents seen by this blog show the cost of the Port Ardley crossing has risen to $3.1 billion, almost double the figure approved by ministers in 2022.
author: Ansel Brackwater
imageCaption: Construction on the eastern approach to the Harbour Bridge in Port Ardley.
body: Opposition parties have called for an independent inquiry into the Harbour Bridge project in Port Ardley after internal documents showed the cost of the crossing has risen to $3.1 billion, nearly double the budget approved four years ago.

The documents, seen by this blog, include a September risk report prepared for the infrastructure ministry that describes the project’s financial controls as “inadequate” and warns that further increases are “likely”.
The bridge, intended to link the city’s container terminal with the northern ring road, was originally due to open in 2026. The latest timetable puts completion in late 2028.
Barnaby Quell, the opposition leader, said ministers had “either not known or not said” how far the project had drifted. “Neither is acceptable,” he told reporters outside parliament.

The infrastructure ministry said cost increases reflected higher steel prices and unexpected ground conditions on the eastern approach, and that it had “kept parliament informed through the usual channels”.
The main contractor, Halverson Kemp, declined to comment on the documents but said it remained committed to delivering the bridge “safely and to the highest standard”.

title: Coffee prices hit record as drought hits growers; cafés weigh price rises
summary: Wholesale arabica has climbed 60 per cent this year. Independent café owners say a $5 flat white may soon be the norm.
author: Petra Wickerly
imageCaption: A barista at work in an independent café in Westmere.
body: Wholesale coffee prices reached a record high this week as prolonged drought in several major growing regions cut harvests and forced roasters to compete for dwindling supplies.
Arabica futures closed at $4.21 a pound on Monday, up about 60 per cent since January. Robusta, the cheaper variety used in instant coffee and many espresso blends, has risen even faster.
For independent cafés, the timing is difficult. Many are still dealing with higher energy bills and rents, and owners say they have already absorbed as much as they can.

body.quote: We’ve held our prices for 18 months. I don’t think we can do it past Christmas.
body.by: Tom Brindlecombe, owner of Grindhouse in Westmere

body: Supermarkets have also begun raising the price of ground and instant coffee, with some own-label products up by a quarter since the summer, according to price tracking by the consumer group Fair Basket.

Traders do not expect relief soon. Rains in the coming months will determine the size of next year’s crop, but analysts say inventories are so low that prices are likely to remain high well into 2027.

title: Inside the factory betting that cheaper batteries will come from salt
summary: Brine Energy’s sodium-ion plant in Calloway will start shipping cells next spring. Its founders say they can undercut lithium by a third.
author: Junia Pelloway
imageCaption: The first production line at Brine Energy’s plant in Calloway.
body: On the edge of an industrial estate in Calloway, behind a fence lined with half-built loading bays, a company called Brine Energy is preparing to do something few people in the battery business thought possible a decade ago: make cells at scale without lithium.

Brine’s batteries use sodium, an element found in ordinary table salt, as the main charge carrier. Sodium-ion cells are heavier and store less energy than the lithium batteries in most electric cars, but they are cheaper, less prone to catching fire and rely on materials that are abundant almost everywhere.

Co-founder Anika Morrowell is careful not to overpromise. “We are not trying to replace lithium in a sports car,” she said during a tour of the plant. “We’re going after grid storage, delivery vans and city cars, where cost matters more than range.”

The company says its cells will cost about a third less per kilowatt-hour than comparable lithium iron phosphate batteries once the factory reaches full output in 2028. Independent analysts are more cautious, but agree the gap is narrowing.

The first production line, capable of producing enough cells each year for about 4,000 home storage systems, is due to start in March. Brine has raised $340 million so far, including a loan from the national infrastructure bank.

body.quote: Nobody thinks about what’s inside their fridge. That’s what we want for batteries.
body.by: Anika Morrowell, co-founder of Brine Energy

title: Three countries sign Seren River water-sharing pact after decade of disputes
summary: The treaty sets minimum flows during the driest months and creates a joint commission to monitor dams upstream.
author: Ivo Starlingford
imageCaption: The Seren River near the border town of Kessa.
body: Three countries that share the Seren River signed a long-awaited water-sharing agreement on Tuesday, ending more than a decade of disputes over dams, irrigation and the dwindling summer flows that millions of farmers rely on.

The treaty, signed at a ceremony in the border town of Kessa, guarantees minimum flow levels during the four driest months of the year and requires each country to give 90 days’ notice before starting any new dam or diversion project.
A joint commission, with its own engineers and a budget funded equally by the three governments, will monitor water levels at 14 stations along the river and publish the data online.

body.quote: The river never cared about our borders. Today, for the first time, our agreements match the river.
body.by: A senior negotiator at the signing ceremony

body: The deal follows two years of talks mediated by a regional development bank. Earlier efforts collapsed in 2019 and again in 2023 amid disagreements over a large hydropower project in the river’s upper reaches.
Farmers’ groups downstream welcomed the agreement but said the real test would come next summer, when the first dry season under the new rules begins.

title: Small-cap stocks rally as retail investors return; analysts urge caution
summary: The index of smaller listed companies is up 9 per cent in a month, its best run since 2021, as trading app sign-ups surge.
author: Rhea Copperfold
imageCaption: Share prices on a trading screen in Halden’s financial district.
body: Shares in smaller companies have had their strongest month in five years, as individual investors return to the market and fund managers rotate out of the large technology stocks that have dominated returns.

The MLX Small Cap index has risen 9.1 per cent since mid-October. More than two-thirds of that gain has come from companies with a market value below $500 million, many of which had lagged the broader market for most of the year.
Data from three of the largest trading platforms shows new account openings rose by about 40 per cent in October compared with September.

“Some of this is a genuine re-rating. Smaller companies were cheap, and they’re less cheap now,” said Joanna Thrale, head of equities at Kessington Asset Management. “But some of it is momentum, and momentum works until it doesn’t.”
Analysts noted that trading volumes in several thinly traded stocks had jumped tenfold in recent weeks, a pattern that has preceded sharp reversals in the past.

title: Marathon champion Ayla Corvane announces retirement at 34
summary: The two-time world champion said she wanted to stop “while running is still a joy”, and will run her final race in Halden in April.
author: Tobin Larkspur
imageCaption: Ayla Corvane during a training run on the hill trails near her home town.
body: Ayla Corvane, the two-time world marathon champion and one of the most decorated distance runners of her generation, announced on Tuesday that she will retire after next spring’s Halden Marathon.
Corvane, 34, made the announcement in a short video posted to her social media accounts, filmed on the hill trails outside her home town where she began running as a teenager.
“I wanted to stop while running is still a joy and not a job,” she said. “I’ve been lucky enough to do this for 16 years. I’d like to finish at home, in front of people who knew me before any of it.”

Corvane won world titles in 2021 and 2023 and set the national record of 2:18:47 in 2022, a mark that still stands. She also took Olympic silver, finishing four seconds behind the winner in one of the closest marathon finishes in the event’s history.
Her coach of 12 years, Piet Hollin, said she had been considering the decision since the summer. “She has nothing left to prove, and she knows it,” he said.
Organisers of the Halden Marathon said they expected record entries for the April race.

title: Astronomers track asteroid’s close pass this weekend; no risk to Earth
summary: The 300-metre rock will pass at about twice the distance of the Moon. Amateur observers with a decent telescope should be able to see it.
author: Linus Quarrendon
imageCaption: The dome of the National Observatory before an overnight observing session.
body: An asteroid roughly the size of a large football stadium will pass close to Earth on Saturday night, giving astronomers a rare opportunity to study an object of its size at relatively short range.

The asteroid, catalogued as 2026 TK4, will come within about 760,000 kilometres of the planet, roughly twice the average distance to the Moon. Space agency scientists said there was no chance of a collision.

It was first detected in early October by a survey telescope and has been tracked by observatories around the world since. Radar observations planned for the weekend should reveal its shape and rotation.

“Objects this size pass this close only every few years,” said Dr Ruth Amberlie of the National Observatory. “It’s a chance to practise exactly the kind of tracking we would need if we ever found one that was actually heading our way.”
Amateur astronomers with a telescope of at least 15 centimetres aperture should be able to spot it as a faint, fast-moving point of light in the eastern sky shortly after midnight.

title: Our cities are built for cars that sit parked 95 per cent of the time
summary: Central Halden gives more land to storing vehicles than to parks and squares. That is a choice, and we can make a different one.
author: Della Fernhaven
imageCaption: A residential street in central Halden.
body: Walk down almost any street in Halden and count the parked cars. Then try to remember when you last saw one of them move.

The average private car is driven for about an hour a day. For the remaining 23, it occupies around 12 square metres of space that, in most of our cities, is handed over free or at a fraction of its value.
A study published last year by the city’s own planning department found that more land in central Halden is devoted to parking than to parks, playgrounds and public squares combined.

body.h: It is not anti-car to say so

body: None of this is an argument for banning cars. Many people need them, especially outside the cities, and will for a long time. It is an argument for pricing space honestly and for asking whether every street really needs to serve as a car park.

Cities that have done this, gradually and street by street, have not collapsed. Shops have generally done better, not worse. Children have somewhere to play. Buses run on time because they aren’t stuck behind someone looking for a space.
We already accept that space in cities is valuable. We just haven’t applied that thinking to the vehicles sitting outside our front doors.

title: Four-day week trial: nurses report less burnout, managers report rota headaches
summary: An evaluation of the six-month pilot at four hospitals found sickness absence fell by a fifth, but filling weekend shifts became harder.
author: Oriel Thistlecombe
imageCaption: Nurses change shifts at Calloway General Hospital.
body: Nurses taking part in a six-month trial of a four-day working week reported lower levels of burnout and took fewer sick days, according to an independent evaluation published on Tuesday. But the report also found that the scheme made rostering significantly more complicated.
The pilot, which ran at four hospitals between March and August, allowed about 600 nurses to work their contracted hours over four longer shifts rather than five. Pay was unchanged.
Sickness absence among participating staff fell by 21 per cent compared with the same period last year. In surveys, 74 per cent said they felt less exhausted at the end of a working week.
However, ward managers said filling weekend and night shifts had become harder, and two of the four hospitals reported an increase in spending on agency staff during the trial.

“The wellbeing results are striking, and we shouldn’t dismiss them,” said Professor Linnea Calloran, who led the evaluation. “But this is not a policy you can switch on without redesigning how wards are staffed.”
The health ministry said it would study the findings before deciding whether to extend the trial.

title: Booksellers report surprise boom in sales of printed maps and atlases
summary: Sales of road atlases and walking maps are up a third this year, driven by younger buyers who say they want to plan trips away from a screen.
author: Otto Fallowfield
imageCaption: Folded walking maps on display in a shop in Halden’s old town.
body: Printed maps, long assumed to be heading the way of the phone directory, are enjoying an unexpected revival, according to figures from the Booksellers Association.

Sales of road atlases, walking maps and illustrated travel maps rose by 34 per cent in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period in 2025. The growth has been strongest among buyers aged 18 to 34.

Booksellers say the trend is partly about travel planning and partly about something harder to measure. “People tell us they like being able to see the whole thing at once,” said Harriet Wexby, who runs a map shop in Halden’s old town. “You don’t get that on a five-inch screen.”

Publishers have responded. Two of the country’s largest map makers have brought back discontinued regional editions this autumn, and a new series of hand-drawn city maps sold out its first print run in a fortnight.
Not everyone is convinced the boom will last. But for now, Ms Wexby says, she is ordering more stock than at any point in the past decade.

title: Rail unions and ministry agree to talks as strike enters second week
summary: Commuters face further disruption on Wednesday, but both sides said they would meet on Thursday for the first time since the walkout began.
author: Teodor Quillane
imageCaption: An empty platform at Halden Central during Monday’s strike.
body: Rail unions and the transport ministry have agreed to hold talks on Thursday, raising hopes of an end to a strike that has disrupted services across much of the country for more than a week.

The meeting, which will be chaired by an independent mediator, will be the first direct contact between the two sides since the Rail and Maritime Union began its walkout over pay and proposed changes to working patterns.
Only about 40 per cent of scheduled passenger services ran on Monday, and freight operators have warned that grain and fuel deliveries could be delayed if the action continues into next week.

Union general secretary Dev Harrowgate said members were “ready to negotiate, not ready to surrender”. Transport Minister Paul Ostergard said he wanted “a fair settlement that the taxpayer can afford”.
Further strikes are scheduled for Wednesday and Friday. Operators advised passengers to check timetables before travelling and to expect crowded trains on routes that are running.

title: How a family bakery became a 40-store chain without outside investors
summary: Lukas Brindell took over his grandmother’s shop in Westmere in 2014. He has turned down every funding offer since, and says it has been worth it.
author: Kesi Ambergate
imageCaption: The original Brindell Bakery shop in Westmere, which still opens at 6am.
body: When Lukas Brindell took over his grandmother’s bakery in Westmere in 2014, it sold about 300 loaves a day and had one oven that, by his own account, “worked when it felt like it”.

Twelve years later, Brindell Bakery has 40 shops across five cities, employs nearly 700 people and expects revenue of about $62 million this year. It has done all of this without selling a single share to an outside investor.
“We had offers. Lots of them,” Mr Brindell said, sitting in the back of the original shop. “Every one of them wanted us to grow faster than we knew how to grow well.”
The company opens no more than four shops a year, each funded from the previous year’s profits. New managers spend at least six months working in an existing branch before they run their own.

The approach has costs. A rival chain backed by private equity has opened more than 90 shops in the same period, and Mr Brindell admits he has lost several prime locations to better-funded competitors.

But he says the slower pace has kept quality consistent and staff turnover low. “My grandmother’s rule was simple: never sell bread you wouldn’t eat yourself,” he said. “It’s much easier to keep that rule with 40 shops than with 400.”

title: How to free up storage on your phone without deleting photos: five simple fixes
summary: Cached app data, old message attachments and offline downloads often take up more space than your camera roll. Here is how to clear them on Android and iPhone.
author: Ilsa Marrowby
imageCaption: Messaging apps are often the largest hidden users of phone storage.
body: Few warnings are as irritating as “storage almost full”, and the instinctive response is to start deleting photos. In most cases, that isn’t necessary. Here are five places to look first, on both Android and iPhone.

Streaming, social media and browser apps store temporary files so they load faster. Over months, these can grow to several gigabytes. On Android, open Settings, then Apps, choose an app and tap Clear cache. On iPhone, the simplest option is to offload and reinstall the worst offenders.

Videos and voice notes in group chats are often the biggest hidden culprit. Most messaging apps include a storage manager that lists large files by conversation, so you can remove them without losing the messages themselves.
Downloaded podcasts, playlists and films are easy to forget about. Check each streaming app’s downloads section and clear anything you have already watched or listened to.
Both operating systems can remove an app while keeping its data, so you can reinstall it later and pick up where you left off. iPhone users can turn this on automatically in Settings under App Store.
Deleted photos and files usually stay on the device for 30 days. Emptying the Recently Deleted album can free up a surprising amount of space immediately.
If you have tried all five and are still short of room, it may be time to move older photos to a computer or cloud backup rather than deleting them outright.

title: Volcano on remote Tarrow Island prompts evacuation of 3,000 residents
summary: Authorities raised the alert level after a swarm of more than 1,500 small earthquakes. Ferries are carrying residents to the mainland.
author: Noor Driftwell
imageCaption: Mount Corran seen from the harbour at Tarrow on Monday morning.
body: Authorities began evacuating about 3,000 people from Tarrow Island on Monday after a sharp increase in seismic activity beneath Mount Corran, the volcano that dominates the island’s northern half.

More than 1,500 small earthquakes were recorded over 48 hours, according to the Geological Survey, which raised the alert level to orange, the second-highest on its four-point scale. Scientists also detected ground swelling of several centimetres on the volcano’s eastern flank.

Two ferries and a navy supply ship are carrying residents to the mainland port of Lisk, a crossing of about four hours. Livestock farmers have been given permission to remain until Wednesday to move animals to the southern end of the island.
“We’re not saying an eruption is certain. We’re saying the signals are strong enough that we would rather people were somewhere safe while we find out,” said volcanologist Dr Arne Kestrelmoor.
Mount Corran last erupted in 1962, when lava flows destroyed two villages but caused no deaths. The island’s only airport has been closed as a precaution.

title: Cup final tickets sell out in 11 minutes as fans criticise resale prices
summary: Some seats were listed on resale sites for more than ten times face value within an hour of the general sale opening.
author: Bram Kettleby
imageCaption: The National Stadium, which will host the cup final on 12 December.
body: Tickets for next month’s National Cup final between Brennick United and Westmere Rovers sold out in 11 minutes on Saturday, and within an hour some were being offered on resale websites for more than ten times their face value.

The football association said more than 210,000 people had joined the online queue for about 38,000 tickets available on general sale. The remainder of the stadium’s 62,000 seats had been allocated to the two clubs, sponsors and grassroots organisations.

Supporters’ groups from both clubs criticised the resale listings, which included a pair of standard seats priced at $1,950 each, and called on the association to cap resale prices, as some other competitions have done.
“This is a final between two working-class clubs, and ordinary fans are being priced out of it,” said Marie Thackwell of the Rovers Supporters’ Trust.
The association said tickets bought through unauthorised resale sites could be cancelled and that it was working with platforms to remove listings that breached its terms.

title: What a small-town newspaper taught me about local democracy
summary: I spent my first three years in journalism covering council meetings and planning rows. It was the most important work I have done.
author: Ida Moorcastle
imageCaption: The former offices of the Brennick Gazette, which closed in 2019.
body: My first job in journalism was at the Brennick Gazette, a weekly paper with a staff of five and a circulation that, on a good week, nudged past 8,000.

I covered planning committees, school board meetings and the annual dispute about the Christmas lights. I wrote about potholes more times than I can count. At the time, I thought of it as an apprenticeship, something to get through before the real work began.
I was wrong. That was the real work.

When a local paper is in the room, councillors know their decisions will be read about. Residents know where to find out what is happening to the field behind their homes. Small mistakes get caught before they become big ones.

The Gazette closed in 2019. Since then, according to residents I still speak to, attendance at council meetings has fallen, and two planning decisions that would once have been front-page news passed with almost no public discussion.
There is no simple fix. But if you have a local paper, subscribe to it. If you don’t, ask who is reporting on the decisions made in your name. If the answer is nobody, that should worry all of us.
